title: The Extra Cable
statement:
A network of n machines, numbered 0 to n - 1, was wired as a tree: connected, with no loop. Then one extra two-way cable was added between two different machines that were not already directly linked. You get all n cables in edges, where edges[i] = [a, b]; note that n is edges.length.

Return a cable whose removal turns the network back into a tree. Several cables usually qualify; return the one that appears last in edges, written exactly as it appears there.

examples.why: The loop is 0–1–2. Removing [2, 3] would cut machine 3 off, so it does not qualify even though it comes last. Among the three loop cables, [0, 2] appears last.
When [1, 2] arrives, both machines have been seen before, but they sit in different pieces, so it joins them instead of closing a loop. Only [3, 0] closes the loop.
All three cables form the loop; the last one is returned in its original orientation, not as [0, 1].

constraints: No pair of machines is linked twice
The cables form a tree plus one extra cable
hints: The extra cable creates exactly one loop. Which cables are candidates, and which candidate is wanted?
Add the cables one by one in input order. The very first cable that links two machines which are already connected is the one that closes the loop. Why is it also the last loop cable in the input?
Use union-find: for each cable, if both ends already have the same root, return that cable; otherwise merge them.

explain.intuition:
A tree plus one cable has exactly one loop, and removing any cable on that loop gives a tree again. Removing a cable off the loop cuts the network in two. So the answer is the loop cable that appears last in the input.

Now add the cables in input order and watch. While the loop is incomplete, every cable joins two pieces that were apart. The loop closes at the moment its last cable arrives, and that cable is the first one whose two ends are already connected. So "last loop cable in the input" equals "first cable that links two already-connected machines". Testing "already connected?" one cable at a time is exactly what union-find does, as built in Count Separate Networks: find both ends, and if the roots match, this cable is redundant. Path compression (here in its one-pass "halving" form, which points each node at its grandparent on the way up) and union by rank make each check nearly O(1). Example 2 shows why "both ends seen before" is not the same test: seen is not connected.
steps: Create a union-find over n = edges.length machines.
If find(a) === find(b), return [a, b]: this cable closes the loop.
Otherwise merge the two sets and continue.
pitfalls: Returning the first cable whose ends were both seen before. Seen is not connected: in example 2, [1, 2] joins two separate pieces.
Returning the last cable in the input. It may hang off the loop, as [2, 3] in example 1, and removing it disconnects the network.
Normalising the cable, for example returning [min, max]. The expected answer is the cable as written, so example 3 wants [1, 0].

solutions.title: Try removing cables from the end
solutions.idea: Walk the cables from last to first. Remove one and run a BFS: the remaining n − 1 cables form a tree exactly when they connect all n machines.

solutions.title: Union-find: the first cable inside one set
solutions.idea: Merge cables in input order. The first one whose ends already share a root closes the loop, and it is the last loop cable in the input.

followups: The cables are now one-way, and the original network was a rooted tree where every machine except the root has exactly one incoming cable. What new cases can the extra cable create?
Return every cable whose removal leaves a tree, not just the last one.
